paper_context.research_question: How can a robust, fast, and accurate neural transition-based parser be developed for full-coverage deep semantic graph representations like Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) and Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR)?
main_claims: The paper introduces the first full-coverage neural semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS).

The proposed neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser, utilizing stack-based embedding features and joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates and token alignments, achieves higher accuracy than attention-based baselines on both MRS and AMR.
The parser is significantly faster (an order of magnitude) than high-precision grammar-based parsers due to incremental prediction and GPU batch processing.
The 86.69% Smatch score achieved by the MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, suggesting MRS as a more attractive semantic representation.
The arc-eager transition system with hard attention and stack-based features is more effective than top-down linearization and soft attention for DMRS parsing.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Parsing accuracy (e.g., F1, Smatch, EDM scores for predicates and arguments)
Parsing speed/efficiency (e.g., tokens per second, batch processing capabilities)
Coverage of semantic representations (e.g., full-coverage for MRS)
Novelty and technical soundness of the proposed neural architecture and transition system
Generalizability to different semantic representations (MRS, EDS, AMR)
Comparison against state-of-the-art and baseline methods

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The common framework for semantic graphs (rooted, labelled, connected, directed graphs with node labels as predicates/concepts and edge labels as arguments/relations) is sufficient to represent MRS-based graphs (DMRS, EDS) and AMR.
supporting_evidence: We define a common framework for semantic graphs, in which we can place both MRSbased graph representations (DMRS and EDS) and AMR.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the framework is not truly common or expressive enough, the comparison and unified parsing approach might be flawed, potentially misrepresenting the capabilities or limitations of the different representations.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The conversion of MRS to DMRS is 'without loss' and DMRS is 'inter-convertible with MRS', implying that parsing DMRS effectively means parsing MRS.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 1 Introduction, Section 2 Deep Meaning Representations
supporting_evidence: We develop parsers for two graph-based conversions of MRS, Elementary Dependency Structure (EDS) (Oepen and Lønning, 2006) and Dependency MRS (DMRS) (Copestake, 2009), of which the latter is inter-convertible with MRS.
MRS can be converted without loss to variablefree dependency graphs, called Dependency MRS (DMRS) (Copestake, 2009; Copestake et al., 2016).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the conversion is not truly lossless or inter-convertible, the claim of 'full-coverage semantic graph parser for MRS' (C1) might be weakened, as the parser is directly operating on DMRS, not raw MRS.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The pre-processing steps, including lemma prediction using an ERG lexicon and Stanford CoreNLP toolkit for tokenization, lemmatization, and NER, provide sufficiently accurate and consistent inputs for the parser.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.3 Lemma prediction, Section 4.1 Sentence encoder
supporting_evidence: We extract a dictionary mapping words to lemmas from the ERG lexicon, which map words to their possible predicates. In combination with a lemmatizer, this can be used to predict a candidate lemma for each token.
We use the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit (Manning et al., 2014) to tokenize and lemmatize sentences, and tag tokens with the Stanford Named Entity Recognizer (Finkel et al., 2005).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Errors or inconsistencies in these pre-processing steps (e.g., incorrect lemmas, POS tags, or NE tags) would propagate to the parser, potentially limiting its performance and making it difficult to isolate the parser's own errors.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The Smatch metric for AMR and EDM for MRS are comparable enough to draw conclusions about the 'attractiveness' of MRS as a semantic representation based on their respective parsing scores and upper bounds.
supporting_evidence: Further, the 86.69% Smatch score of our MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, making MRS an attractive choice as a semantic representation.
EDM can be contrasted with the Smatch metric (Cai and Knight, 2013) for evaluating AMR graphs.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If Smatch and EDM measure fundamentally different aspects or have different sensitivities, then directly comparing scores (C4) to suggest one representation is 'more attractive' might be misleading or invalid.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The oracle for the transition system, which delays reduce actions where possible, provides an optimal or near-optimal sequence for training the parser.
supporting_evidence: In our model the oracle delays reduce, where possible, until the end alignment of the stack top node spans the node on the buffer. As the span end alignments often cover phrases that they head (e.g. for quantifiers) this gives a natural interpretation to predicting the span end together with the reduce action.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: A suboptimal oracle could lead to a parser that learns suboptimal transition sequences, limiting its maximum achievable accuracy, especially for complex graph structures or non-planar dependencies.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The DeepBank dataset, derived from the ERG, is a representative and sufficiently diverse corpus for evaluating MRS parsing, despite being restricted to sentences parsable by the ERG.
supporting_evidence: DeepBank (Flickinger et al., 2012) is HPSG and MRS annotation of the Penn Treebank Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus text...

Parses are only provided for sentences for which the ERG has an analysis acceptable to the annotator – this means that we cannot evaluate parsing accuracy for sentences which the ERG cannot parse (approximately 15% of the original corpus).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The reported accuracy for MRS parsing (C2) might be an overestimate of real-world performance if the test set is inherently 'easier' due to its restriction to ERG-parsable sentences, limiting generalizability to out-of-grammar inputs.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The automatically-obtained alignments for AMR using the JAMR aligner are sufficiently accurate for training and evaluating the AMR parser.
supporting_evidence: For AMR parsing we use LDC2015E86... We obtain alignments using the rule-based JAMR aligner (Flanigan et al., 2014).
The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Noise or inaccuracies in these alignments could hinder the AMR parser's performance, especially for models sensitive to alignment quality (e.g., arc-eager), potentially masking the true potential of the proposed architecture for AMR (C2).

chaining_notes: The paper explicitly contrasts its approach with previous grammar-based MRS parsing (Toutanova et al., 2005) which had high precision but incomplete coverage, positioning itself as a robust, full-coverage alternative.
The comparison of MRS parsing performance to AMR's upper-bound is a key argument for MRS's attractiveness, which might warrant deeper scrutiny regarding metric comparability.
The paper highlights the importance of unlexicalized predicates for generalization and training efficiency, which is a specific design choice with empirical backing.
The use of hard attention based on supervised alignments is a deliberate choice, contrasted with soft attention, and its effectiveness is claimed for the arc-eager system.

The paper acknowledges that its AMR parser, while outperforming some neural baselines, still lags behind state-of-the-art AMR parsers that leverage extensive external resources, suggesting a potential area for future work or a limitation of the current 'end-to-end' scope.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically structured argument for a novel neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser designed for deep semantic graph representations, specifically Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) and Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). The paper effectively moves from identifying a gap in robust, full-coverage deep semantic parsing to proposing a detailed technical solution. It systematically evaluates architectural choices, providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of stack-based features, hard attention, and unlexicalized predicates. The argument for MRS as an 'attractive' representation, based on parsing performance relative to AMR, forms a key concluding point. While the overall flow is coherent, some claims, particularly those involving cross-metric comparisons or generalizability from restricted datasets, warrant closer scrutiny regarding their underlying assumptions and the strength of their evidence linkage.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Existing deep semantic parsing approaches (grammar-based or shallow neural) suffer from incomplete coverage, lack of robustness, or slow processing for linguistically expressive representations like MRS.
C1: A robust, fast, and accurate full-coverage neural parser is needed for deep semantic graphs (MRS, AMR) to advance Natural Language Understanding.

M1: Propose a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser that uses stack-based embedding features, hard attention with pointer networks, and jointly predicts unlexicalized predicates and token alignments.
Sub-argument M1.1: MRS-based graphs (DMRS, EDS) and AMR can be unified under a common framework of rooted, labeled, connected, directed graphs, enabling a single parsing approach.
Sub-argument M1.2: DMRS is inter-convertible with MRS without loss, allowing the parser to achieve 'full-coverage' for MRS by parsing DMRS.
Sub-argument M1.3: An arc-eager transition system, adapted for graph parsing and non-planar dependencies, is employed for incremental graph generation.
Sub-argument M1.4: Hard attention, predicting alignments with a pointer network, and explicit conditioning on stack-based features, are more effective than soft attention or simpler linearizations.
Sub-argument M1.5: Predicting unlexicalized predicates (with pre-predicted lemmas) improves generalization to sparse/unseen predicates and speeds up training.
E1: Empirical evaluation is conducted on DeepBank (for DMRS/EDS) and LDC2015E86 (for AMR), using EDM and Smatch metrics respectively.
R1 (C2): The proposed parser achieves higher accuracy than attention-based encoder-decoder baselines on both MRS (DMRS/EDS) and AMR benchmarks.
R2 (C3): The parser is significantly faster (an order of magnitude) than high-precision grammar-based parsers due to incremental prediction and GPU batch processing.
R3 (C5): The arc-eager transition system with hard attention and stack-based features is empirically shown to be more effective than top-down linearization and soft attention for DMRS parsing.
R4 (C6): Unlexicalized models are more accurate and faster to train due to better generalization and smaller decoder output vocabulary.
R5 (C7): Different predicate orderings (monotone vs. in-order) are optimal for DMRS and AMR respectively, suggesting representation-specific linearization preferences.
R6 (C4): The 86.69% Smatch score for MRS parsing is higher than the reported upper-bound on AMR parsing (83% F1), suggesting MRS as a more attractive semantic representation.
Conclusion: The paper successfully develops a robust, fast, and wide-coverage neural parser for deep semantic representations, advancing the state of parsing and highlighting the potential of MRS.

strengths.title: Clear Problem Statement and Motivation
strengths.description: The introduction clearly articulates the limitations of previous approaches to deep semantic parsing (incomplete coverage, slow grammar-based systems) and effectively motivates the need for a robust, fast, and full-coverage neural solution. This sets a strong foundation for the proposed work.

Abstract: 'Yet statistical parsing has focussed almost exclusively on bilexical dependencies or domain-specific logical forms.'

strengths.title: Systematic Architectural Comparison and Empirical Validation
strengths.description: The paper systematically evaluates different architectural components, including linearization strategies (top-down vs. arc-eager), attention mechanisms (soft vs. hard), and feature sets (vanilla vs. stack-based). The empirical results (Tables 1, 2, 5) provide clear evidence supporting the design choices, strengthening the claim-to-evidence linkage for the proposed model's effectiveness.

Section 5.4 MRS parsing results: 'Next we consider models that predict the alignments with pointer networks, contrasting soft and hard attention models (Table 2).'
Section 5.4 MRS parsing results: 'The arc-eager stack-based architecture improves further over the model that purely relies on the hard attention (Table 2).'

strengths.title: Strong Evidence for Speed Improvement
strengths.description: The paper provides compelling quantitative evidence for the significant speed advantage of the proposed neural parser over a high-precision grammar-based parser (ACE). The comparison of tokens per second for both batched and unbatched versions clearly supports the claim of being 'an order of magnitude faster'.

strengths.description: The establishment of a common framework for semantic graphs in Section 2 provides a strong conceptual basis for applying the same parsing methodology to both MRS-based representations (DMRS, EDS) and AMR. This enhances the coherence of the overall argument and demonstrates the generalizability of the approach.

concerns.title: Ambiguity in 'MRS Smatch' and Comparability with AMR Upper-Bound
concerns.description: The claim (C4) that the MRS parser's 86.69% Smatch score is 'higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing' (83% F1) is presented as evidence for MRS being a 'more attractive' representation. However, the paper primarily uses EDM for MRS evaluation and Smatch for AMR. The origin and calculation of the 86.69% Smatch score for MRS are not explicitly detailed, making a direct comparison to an AMR inter-annotator agreement upper bound (typically also Smatch) potentially misleading without a clear statement on metric equivalence or a more nuanced interpretation of 'attractiveness'. This weakens the logical coherence of the comparative argument.
evidence: Abstract: 'Further, the 86.69% Smatch score of our MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, making MRS an attractive choice as a semantic representation.'
Section 5.2 Evaluation: 'EDM can be contrasted with the Smatch metric (Cai and Knight, 2013) for evaluating AMR graphs.'
Section 1 Introduction: 'inter-annotator agreement has been shown to be relatively low [for AMR], placing on upper bound of 83% F1 on the expected parser performance.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explicitly clarify how the 86.69% Smatch score for MRS was derived and discuss the methodological implications of comparing it directly to an AMR inter-annotator agreement upper bound. Provide a more cautious or qualified interpretation of 'attractiveness' if direct metric comparability cannot be fully established.

concerns.title: Limited Generalizability of MRS Accuracy Due to Data Restrictions
concerns.description: The DeepBank dataset used for MRS parsing is restricted to sentences parsable by the ERG, which accounts for approximately 85% of the original corpus (Assumption A6). While acknowledged, this means the reported high MRS parsing accuracies (C2) are on an inherently 'easier' subset of natural language. This limitation impacts the claim of a 'robust, full-coverage' parser (C1) as its performance on out-of-grammar or unparsable sentences remains unevaluated, potentially overstating real-world applicability.
evidence: Section 5.1 Data: 'Parses are only provided for sentences for which the ERG has an analysis acceptable to the annotator – this means that we cannot evaluate parsing accuracy for sentences which the ERG cannot parse (approximately 15% of the original corpus).'

Section 5.4 MRS parsing results: 'Despite the promising performance of the model there is still a gap between the accuracy of our parser and ACE. One reason for this is that the test set sentences will arguably be easier for ACE to parse as their choice was restricted by the grammar that ACE uses.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the implications of the DeepBank data selection more prominently in the results and conclusion sections, perhaps by estimating potential performance drop on unparsable sentences or outlining future work on handling out-of-grammar inputs for MRS parsing.

This suggests that the AMR evaluation might be constrained by data quality issues, potentially masking the true capabilities of the proposed arc-eager architecture for AMR parsing and qualifying the claim of 'higher accuracy than attention-based baselines on both MRS and AMR' (C2).

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both papers address large-scale semantic parsing and represent meaning as graphs. Reddy et al. conceptualize it as a graph matching problem using CCG output, focusing on Freebase grounding. This paper, in contrast, uses a transition-based neural approach for deep linguistic representations (MRS, AMR) and supervised parsing.

This paper explicitly cites Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016) as inspiration for incorporating stack-based features in dependency parsing. Both utilize BiLSTM for sentence encoding and transition-based parsing. The key difference is that Kiperwasser and Goldberg focus on syntactic dependency parsing, while this paper extends the approach to complex semantic graphs, including node generation and non-planar dependencies.

Both papers propose arc-eager AMR parsers. However, this paper states that Damonte et al.'s system is 'more narrowly defined for AMR graphs,' implying a more generalizable approach in the current work. The current paper also demonstrates improved performance over previous sequence-to-sequence AMR parsers, which would include Damonte et al.

concerns.title: Incomparability of Evaluation Metrics for Cross-Representation Claims
concerns.description: The paper directly compares Smatch scores for AMR parsing with EDM scores for MRS parsing to argue that MRS is a 'more attractive' semantic representation (Claim C4). Smatch and EDM are fundamentally different metrics: Smatch is alignment-agnostic and finds an optimal 1-1 node mapping, while EDM is span-based and relies on explicit alignments. Their numerical values are not directly comparable in a way that allows for conclusions about the inherent 'attractiveness' or quality of the underlying semantic representation. This undermines the validity of Claim C4.
evidence: Abstract: 'Further, the 86.69% Smatch score of our MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, making MRS an attractive choice as a semantic representation.'

Section 5.2 Evaluation: 'EDM can be contrasted with the Smatch metric (Cai and Knight, 2013) for evaluating AMR graphs. This evaluation does not rely on sentence alignments; instead it performs inference over graph alignments to estimate the maximum F1-score obtainable from a 1-1 matching between the predicted and gold graph nodes.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Reframe the comparison between MRS and AMR parsing performance. Instead of directly comparing numerical scores across different metrics, discuss the strengths and weaknesses of each representation and parsing approach independently, or propose a unified, representation-agnostic evaluation framework if such a comparison is desired.

concerns.title: Dataset Bias and Limited Generalizability for MRS Parsing
concerns.description: The DeepBank dataset used for MRS parsing is restricted to sentences for which the ERG (English Resource Grammar) has an acceptable analysis. This means approximately 15% of the original corpus is excluded. This selection bias likely inflates the reported accuracy for MRS parsing, as the test set is inherently 'easier' for grammar-based systems or systems trained on grammar-derived data. Consequently, the claim of a 'robust' and 'full-coverage' parser (C1) might not generalize well to real-world inputs that fall outside the ERG's coverage.
evidence: Section 5.1 Data: 'Parses are only provided for sentences for which the ERG has an analysis acceptable to the annotator – this means that we cannot evaluate parsing accuracy for sentences which the ERG cannot parse (approximately 15% of the original corpus).'
Section 5.4 MRS parsing results: 'One reason for this is that the test set sentences will arguably be easier for ACE to parse as their choice was restricted by the grammar that ACE uses.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge the limitations of the DeepBank dataset more explicitly in the discussion of results. If possible, provide an analysis of performance on a small set of sentences outside ERG coverage, or discuss strategies for handling out-of-grammar inputs to support the 'robust' claim.

concerns.title: Impact of Noisy Alignments on AMR Parsing Evaluation
concerns.description: The paper explicitly hypothesizes that noise in the automatically-obtained AMR alignments (from the rule-based JAMR aligner) negatively impacts the arc-eager model's performance for AMR parsing. This introduces a significant confounding factor, making it difficult to accurately assess the true efficacy of the proposed architecture for AMR and compromising the comparison between arc-eager and top-down linearizations for AMR.
evidence: Section 5.1 Data: 'We obtain alignments using the rule-based JAMR aligner (Flanigan et al., 2014).'
Section 5.5 AMR parsing: 'The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify the level of noise in the AMR alignments if possible, or perform an error analysis to demonstrate its impact. Consider experimenting with different alignment strategies or a small set of manually verified alignments to validate the hypothesis and mitigate this limitation.

concerns.title: Potential Lossiness in Top-down Reentrancy Handling
concerns.description: The paper states that the top-down linearization's representation of reentrancies is 'potentially lossy' and recovered 'heuristically.' This raises concerns about the fidelity and accuracy of the semantic graphs produced by this linearization strategy, especially for complex MRS structures that frequently involve reentrancies. While the arc-eager model is preferred, the methodological weakness of the top-down baseline should be noted.
evidence: Section 3.1 Top-down linearization: 'Our potentially lossy representation represents the edge by repeating the label and alignment of the dependen node, which is recovered heuristically.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide more details on the heuristic recovery process and its empirical impact on reentrancy accuracy for the top-down model. If the top-down model is used as a baseline, its limitations in representing complex graph structures should be clearly articulated.

concerns.title: Limited Transparency in Hyperparameter Tuning
concerns.description: While the paper mentions using grid search and heuristic search for hyperparameter tuning, the specific ranges explored, the number of trials, and the exact criteria for selecting the 'best performance' are not fully detailed. This lack of transparency makes it challenging for other researchers to reproduce the exact model setup and verify the optimality of the chosen parameters, impacting reproducibility.
evidence: Section 5.3 Model Setup: 'This configuration, found using grid search and heuristic search within the range of models that fit into a single GPU, gave the best performance on the development set under multiple graph linearizations.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a more detailed appendix or supplementary material outlining the hyperparameter search space, the number of iterations or trials, and the specific objective function used for selection (e.g., EDM F1 on dev set).

concerns.title: Unverified Optimality of Transition System Oracle
concerns.description: The oracle for the arc-eager transition system delays reduce actions 'where possible' until the end alignment of the stack top node spans the buffer node. While this is a reasonable heuristic, the paper does not provide a formal proof or extensive empirical analysis of its optimality or near-optimality, especially for handling highly non-planar dependencies or complex graph structures. A suboptimal oracle could limit the parser's learning capacity and maximum achievable accuracy.
evidence: Section 3.2 Arc-eager parsing: 'In our model the oracle delays reduce, where possible, until the end alignment of the stack top node spans the node on the buffer.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the theoretical implications of the oracle's greedy choices for complex graph structures. If possible, provide an analysis of oracle error rates or compare against alternative oracle strategies to demonstrate its effectiveness.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a significant incremental advancement in semantic parsing by adapting and refining established neural encoder-decoder and transition-based parsing paradigms for deep semantic graph representations, specifically Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) and Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). The core contribution lies in extending these neural methods, which have seen success in dependency and constituency parsing, to the more complex task of full-coverage MRS parsing, a domain previously dominated by high-precision, but often incomplete, grammar-based systems. The paper refines the neural architecture by integrating stack-based embedding features, hard attention mechanisms, and joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates and token alignments within an arc-eager transition system. This reorganization of existing neural components for a new, challenging target representation yields a parser that is demonstrably faster than grammar-based alternatives and achieves higher accuracy than attention-based neural baselines on both MRS (DMRS/EDS) and AMR. The work effectively bridges the gap between robust, fast neural parsing and linguistically deep, complex semantic representations, offering a viable and efficient alternative to existing approaches.

Neural encoder-decoder transition-based parsers, leveraging RNNs for global conditioning, can robustly parse complex structures without increasing algorithmic complexity.

Incremental prediction and GPU batch processing make the parser significantly faster than high-precision grammar-based parsers.
The high Smatch score for MRS parsing, exceeding the upper-bound for AMR, suggests MRS is a more attractive semantic representation for parsing.
Unlexicalized models are more accurate due to generalization and faster to train due to smaller vocabularies.
Different linearization orderings (monotone vs. in-order) are more effective for DMRS and AMR respectively, indicating representation-specific optimal strategies.

strengths.title: Successful Adaptation of Neural Paradigms to MRS
strengths.description: The paper successfully adapts and integrates established neural parsing techniques (encoder-decoder, transition-based parsing, stack-based features, hard attention, pointer networks) to the challenging and less-explored domain of full-coverage Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS). evidence: We propose a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser which is the first full-coverage semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS).
The model architecture uses stack-based embedding features, predicting graphs jointly with unlexicalized predicates and their token alignments.

Our parser is a transition-based model for parsing semantic graphs. However, instead of generating arcs over an ordered, fixed set of nodes (the words in the sentence), we generate the nodes, including their labels and alignments to the input tokens, jointly with the transition actions.
We use a variant of the arc-eager transition-system that is able to parse graphs and non-planar dependencies.

strengths.title: Demonstrated Efficiency and Speed Improvement

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser designed for full-coverage deep semantic graph representations, specifically Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) and Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). The core conceptual shift lies in applying a robust, fast, and end-to-end neural approach to MRS parsing, a domain traditionally dominated by high-precision but often incomplete grammar-based systems. The proposed architecture integrates stack-based embedding features, hard attention for token alignments, and joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates. The authors claim this is the first full-coverage neural MRS parser, demonstrating significant speed improvements (an order of magnitude) over grammar-based parsers and higher accuracy than attention-based baselines on both MRS (DMRS/EDS) and AMR. A notable, potentially disruptive, claim is that the MRS parser's Smatch score surpasses the established upper-bound for AMR parsing, positioning MRS as a more attractive semantic representation. The paper systematically evaluates different linearization strategies and attention mechanisms, providing empirical evidence for the efficacy of the arc-eager transition system with stack-based features and unlexicalized predicates.
logical_argument_graph: The paper identifies a gap: existing deep semantic parsers are either grammar-based (high precision, incomplete coverage for MRS) or neural (shallow, limited to bilexical dependencies).
It proposes a novel neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser to address this, aiming for robustness, speed, and full coverage for linguistically deep semantic graphs like MRS and AMR.
The proposed architecture employs a bidirectional RNN encoder and a transition-based decoder (arc-eager variant) that incrementally generates graph nodes, their labels, and token alignments.

Key architectural innovations include stack-based embedding features, hard attention via pointer networks for alignments, and joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates for generalization and efficiency.

The model is evaluated on DMRS/EDS (conversions of MRS) and AMR datasets, using EDM and Smatch metrics respectively, and compared against neural attention-based baselines and traditional grammar-based parsers (ACE).
Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed arc-eager stack-based model achieves higher accuracy than neural baselines on both MRS and AMR.
The parser is shown to be significantly faster (an order of magnitude) than grammar-based parsers due to incremental prediction and GPU batch processing.

A comparative analysis of MRS and AMR parsing performance leads to the claim that MRS is a more attractive semantic representation, citing its achieved Smatch score exceeding AMR's theoretical upper bound.
The paper concludes that deep learning can enable robust, fast, and full-coverage parsing of complex semantic representations like MRS in an end-to-end fashion, opening new research avenues.
Specific design choices, such as unlexicalized models and monotone ordering for DMRS, are justified by improved accuracy and training speed.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for deep semantic graph representations, specifically Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) and Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). The core reasoning is that by combining stack-based embedding features, hard attention for token alignments, and joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates within an arc-eager transition system, it's possible to achieve robust, fast, and accurate parsing for complex semantic representations. The paper systematically evaluates these architectural choices, demonstrating empirical improvements over attention-based baselines and significant speed advantages over grammar-based parsers for MRS. A key argument is also made for MRS's "attractiveness" compared to AMR, based on parsing performance relative to an estimated upper bound, though this claim warrants careful scrutiny regarding metric comparability.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: Existing deep semantic parsers for MRS are high-precision but incomplete (grammar-based) or shallow (bilexical dependencies). AMR parsing also faces limitations (data size, inter-annotator agreement).
Proposed Solution: Develop a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for full-coverage deep semantic graphs (MRS, AMR).

Architectural Innovations: Integrate stack-based embedding features, hard attention with pointer networks for token alignments, joint prediction of unlexicalized predicates and token alignments, and an arc-eager transition system for graphs and non-planar dependencies.

Hypothesized Benefits: Achieve robustness and full coverage for MRS, higher accuracy than attention-based baselines, significantly faster than grammar-based parsers (due to incremental prediction and GPU batching), improved generalization and training speed with unlexicalized models, and optimized performance with specific linearization strategies (monotone for DMRS, in-order for AMR).

Empirical Validation (MRS/DMRS/EDS): Demonstrate improved F1 over attention-based baselines (e.g., 79.68% to 84.16% F1 for DMRS), show an order-of-magnitude speedup over ACE (529.42 tps vs 7.47 tps), confirm unlexicalized models are more accurate and faster, and validate the effectiveness of arc-eager with hard attention and stack features, with monotone ordering performing better for DMRS.

Empirical Validation (AMR): Achieve 60.11% Smatch, an 8% improvement over an existing neural AMR parser, outperform the JAMR baseline and other sequence-to-sequence parsers, but acknowledge lagging behind state-of-the-art (SOTA) parsers that use extensive external resources, with in-order linearization performing better for AMR.
Comparative Claim: MRS is a more attractive semantic representation, evidenced by its parser achieving a Smatch score (86.69% or 86.50%) that is higher than AMR's estimated upper-bound of 83% F1.
Conclusion: The proposed parser advances deep semantic parsing by providing a robust, fast, and wide-coverage neural solution for MRS and demonstrating strong performance on AMR.

consensus_findings: The proposed neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser is acknowledged as the first full-coverage neural semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS), representing a significant novelty and advancement.

There is strong agreement that the parser achieves significantly faster processing speeds (an order of magnitude) compared to high-precision grammar-based parsers, attributed to incremental prediction and GPU batch processing.
Reviewers consistently find empirical evidence supporting the claim that the proposed parser achieves higher accuracy than attention-based baselines on both MRS (DMRS/EDS) and AMR.

The systematic comparison and empirical validation of architectural choices, including linearization strategies (top-down vs. arc-eager), attention mechanisms (soft vs. hard), and feature sets (lexicalized vs. unlexicalized, stack-based features), are recognized as a strength.
The effectiveness of the arc-eager transition system with hard attention and stack-based features for DMRS parsing is well-supported by empirical results.
The empirical justification for using unlexicalized models, citing improved accuracy due to generalization and faster training, is consistently noted.
The paper's establishment of a common framework for semantic graphs (MRS-based and AMR) is seen as a strength, enabling a unified parsing approach.

The impact of noise in automatically-obtained AMR alignments on the arc-eager model's performance for AMR parsing is a hypothesized factor, making it difficult to accurately assess the true efficacy of the proposed architecture for AMR.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Given this rep- resentation, we conceptualize semantic pars- ing as a graph matching problem. Our model converts sentences to semantic graphs using CCG and subsequently grounds them to Free- base guided by denotations as a form of weak supervision. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: As a fresh reviewer, you should form your own opinion of the paper. Note that you will not initially see the previous reviews or the authors’ revision notes (new in August 2023), but after you submit your review, you will gain access to the old reviews and the revision notes (click on the “Previous URL” link in the submission metadata). At this point, you should check the revision notes to see whether any weaknesses in your review were previously identified, and if so, edit your review to explain why the revisions were not fully adequate to address the weaknesses in question. You may also consider whether the previous reviews identified weaknesses that you hadn’t thought of, and if so, whether you agree that they represent serious concerns meriting inclusion in your review.

In this paper, we build a semantic parser that does not require example annotations or question-answer pairs but instead learns from a large knowledge base (KB) and web-scale cor- pora. Speciﬁcally, we exploit Freebase, a large community-authored knowledge base that spans many sub-domains and stores real world facts in graphical format, and parsed sentences from a large corpus. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
